ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Seizure of naptha in Gujarat 
*641.SHRI R.K.ANAND:† 
SHRIMATIPREMACARIAPPA: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Anti-Adulteration Cell had seized a ledger of a 
company which produces naphtha in Gujarat showing details of purchases of benzene 
and toluene; and 
(b) if so, whether Government have initiated any inquiry to find out details of those oil 
PSUs who are colluding in adulteration by callously selling petro-products like 
naptha to operators? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUMAND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) After the AAC was wound up on 31 July, 2004, the documents of the Anti-
Adulteration Cell (AAC) were passed on to the Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell under 
the aegis of the Ministry of Petroleum and Natural Gas. No ledger has been found 
pertaining to any Gujarat-based naptha producing company showing details of purchases 
of benzene and toluene. 
†The question was actually asked on the floor of the House by Shri R.K. Anand. 
 
 
 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
It may be noted that several files of the AAC have been seized by the Central 
Bureau of Investigation. 
(b) The following are the major steps taken by the Government/Public Sector 
Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) towards containing adulteration, including 
adulteration on account of the diversion of naphtha for unauthorized use: 
(i) In accordance with the Control Or ders issued by the Government 
under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, to prevent fuel 
adulteration, State Governments are empowered to take action 
against those indulging in adulteration. Government have 
repeatedly urged State Governments/Union Territory Administrations 
to step up inspections/surprise checks to ensure that adulteration 
related activities are minimized and to exercise vigil/conduct 
inspections at various private firms, factories, processing units, 
etc. under their jurisdictions to identify the perpetrators of 
adulteration and take stringent action against them within the 
available legal framework. 
(ii) OMCs undertake regular and surprise inspections of Retail outlets 
and also take action under Ma rketing Discipline Guidelines 
(MDG) and Dealership Agreements against those i ndulging in 
adulteration and malpractices. MDG provide for penalty of 
termination of dealership in case of adulteration being established. 
(iii) As advised by the Government, Oil Marketing Companies 
(OMCs) have created a separate wing to report to a Director other 
than Director (Marketing), whic h will oversee and monitor all 
activities and operations to curb adulteration and specify norms 
and guidelines in this regard. 
(iv) Keeping in view the misuse/diversion of SKO for adulteration, the 
import of SKO by private parties has been canalized through OMCs. 
(v) OMCs have introduced new ta mper-proof tank-truck locking 
systems to prevent en route adulteration by transporters. 
(vi) IT solutions like monitoring movement of tank trucks through 
Global Positioning System (GPS) and monitoring the level of 
2 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
fuel tanks in Retail Outlets through retail automation are being introduced. 
(vii) Branding of Retail Outlets and third party certification of Retail Outlets 
have been initiated by the OMCs. 
(viii) A pilot project covering 10% of blocks in the country has been recently 
approved by the Government for strengthening the distribution network of 
PDS kerosene with a view to working towards ensuring that this product 
is made available to the targeted consumers and is not diverted for 
adulteration. The Scheme proposes setting up wholesale storage facilities 
at block level, with storage tanks and calibrated dispensing units; creation of 5-
10 sub-wholesale points within the block to facilitate deliveries to retail 
outlets; and involving Panchayati Raj Institutions in monitoring the 
implementation of the scheme. The details are being worked out. 
Measures to check adulteration are ke pt under continuous review of the 
Government. 
SHRI R.K. ANAND: The hon. Minister has given an elaborate reply. This Anti-
Adulteration Cell was created in view of the active vigilance of the Oil Coordination 
Committee. Is it a fact that the Anti-adulteration Cell and the Oil Coordination 
Committee were disbanded in June, 2004, in view of the fact that officials of the Cell 
were caught taking money from those who adulterate petrol, diesel and other 
lubricants? 
SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, the Oil Coordination Committee and the 
Anti-Adulteration Cell are two completely different institutions. They were removed for 
completely different reasons. The Oil Coordination Committee was removed because 
there is no longer any need to do oil coordination once we removed, or, at least, 
announced, dismantling the APM system. In so far as ACC is concerned, it is true that 
two officers were caught by the CBI and investigation is going on. We had also found 
that the real issues involved in adulteration were not being answered by the Anti-
Adulteration Cell; and instead they were merely duplicating the work that is really the 
responsibility of the State Government and the oil marketing companies themselves. 
So, a one-man Committee was set up which went into a number of representations we had 
received from several 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
different sources and that Committee recommended that the AAC should be 
wound up and we have done that. Simultaneously, we have taken a number of 
complementary measures to deal with the menace of adulteration. 
SHRIR K. ANAND: Sir, Kerosene and Naphtha are the two ingredients which 
are used for adulteration of petrol and diesel. Naphtha is being imported from 
Dubai. I would like to know from the hon. Minister whether the Government 
has conducted any inquiry how Naphtha and Kerosene are going into the hands 
of the people who adulterate diesel and petrol , because they are making a 
profit of Rs. 7,000 to Rs. 8,000 per 1,000 litres of petrol and diesel. 
SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, the import of Naphtha has been 
freed ever since the announcement of the APM dismantling. So, it is true that it is 
being imported. At the same time, we have a very stringent Control Order relating 
to Naphtha, which requires licences to  be obtained from the appropriate 
authority of the State or the district as the case may be, as well as the provision 
of end-user certificate. So, while there is a pretty firm control over what 
happens with respect to Naphtha, Benzene and Toluene are the two products 
that are not included in the Control Order. And, therefore, control over what is 
happening with them is substantially less than, perhaps, it ought to be. Because, as 
I have found, way, back in November, 2000, it was reported by the Bhatnagar 
Committee that there ought  it to be the exclusion of these two because the 
difference between their prices and that of MS and HSD was not very significant. 
Since then, there have been a number of changes but, appropriate action was 
not taken by the previous Government in this regard. 
With respect to Kerosene, we did have a parallel marketing system but 
we have stopped that now and any import of SKO is canalised through the 
OMCs.  
SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: Sir, the hon. Minister has given a 
 detailed reply and also said that the Anti-adulteration Cell of the Ministry 
was wound up on 31st July, 2004, and the new has not yet been constituted. 
But, there are so many agencies looking after the same thing, namely Petroleum 
Planning and Analysis Wing, Oil Marketing Companies, and so on. I would like to 
know from the hon. Minister whether it is true that there is no coordination 
among these agencies of the Petroleum Ministry, oil companies 
4 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and State Governments, resulting in rampant practice of adulteration in petroleum 
products. I would like to know how much losses are being caused to the national 
exchequer due to adulteration. I also would like to know from the hon. Minister whether 
the Government proposes to have one authority to check and crackdown on the 
adulteration racket being run throughout the country. 
SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, I will be very grateful if the hon. Member 
could answer her own question becuase, precisely, there is no way of establishing the 
quantum of adulteration that is taking place. Everybody is free to throw around his 
own figure. As far as the Anti-adulteration Cell is concerned, its work has not been 
transferred to the PPAC. All that has happened is, the record, of the AAC have been transferred 
there because it was found that the AAC, as an institution, was not serving any useful purpose. 
And, since some of its officers had been found involved in malpractices, we felt that there 
was no point in continuing with that particular institution. As regards coordination, 
there is considerable coordination between the Centre and the States. But, eventually, 
the powers, conferred under the Essential Commodities Act by the Ministry of Petroleum on 
the State Governments, have to be exercised by the State Governments, and by the 
authorities below them at the district and the sub-district level. So, that is a part of the 
administrative measures to be taken. But so far as the difference between the prices of the 
adulterants and the price of the product that is adulterated is concerned, so long as there is 
a substantial differences between the prices of the two the temptation to conduct such 
adulteration will always be there. It would require a full debate to explain all the steps 
that we have taken in this regard; and I would welcome an opportunity to be able to 
explain this in much greater details.

DR. K. MALAISAMY: Sir, despite the AAC and the OMCC, 
supplemented by the hon. Minister's co mplementary efforts, the fact remains 
that the incidents of adulteration are on  the increase. Particularly, mixing of 
kerosene with petrol and diesel is a very common practice. In the light of this 
backgrond, I would like to ask the hon. Minister whether our system is 
inadequate or ineffective. 
SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Mr. Chairman, Sir, our system is 
inadequate, but not ineffective. We are, therefore, continuously reviewing what 
steps can be taken. But the fundamental fact is that so long as we attempt to 
protect our consumers and our citizens from the full impact of the rise in 
international prices on some sensitive petroleum products, but not on others, 
thereby, creating, and, sometimes, widening the gap between these adulterants and 
the product that is adulterated, there will be a temptation on the part of 
unscrupulous elements who are, unfortunately, very large in our commercial 
community, to indulge in these malpractices. But we have armed our State 
Governments with the powers that they re quire in order to be able to tackle 
this menace. And to the extent to which State Governments including the State 
Government of Tamil Nadu, which is run by the Party to which the hon. 
Member belongs, act in full consciousness and full utilisation of their powers, 
this menace can be effectively tackled. At the same time, there are steps that we 
can take to improve the distribution system, to ensure that the product reaches 
the intended consumer or the intended be neficiary. We are engaged, at the 
moment, in elaborating a pilot project for kerosene, which, I think, will have a 
major impact on the adulteration of diesel. Now that this information has come to 
our attention, I think, with respect to benzene and toluene also we should be 
taking some special steps to stop this menace.

SHRI HARISH RAWAT: 
Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to state: 
(a) the quantum of grants/bans received by Central autonomous bodies 
during the year 2002-2003;

8 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
   
(b) the purpose for which these grants/loans were sanctioned to these bodies; 
and 
(c) in what manner Government ensure the proper utilization of the 
grants/loans in the absence of utilization certificates? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (SHRI P. CHIDAMABARAM): (a) to (c) 
A Statement is laid on the table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) The provisions of the General Financial Rules stipulate that each 
Ministry/Department is empowered to sanction grants/loans to central autonomous 
bodies conforming to the objectives of the organisation concerned and its 
approved pattern of assistance. It is  the responsibility of the sanctioning 
Ministry concerned to ensure proper utilisation of the assistance provided and 
obtain Utilisation Certificates related thereto. The accounts of the grantee 
institutions are open to inspection by the sanctioning authority/audit whenever 
called upon. If Utilisation Certificates are not received, the Ministries 
concerned are expected not to sanction fresh grants, and may blacklist the 
organisation from receiving future grants, subsidy or any other type of financial 
support from the Government. Overall and detailed information related to 
question, purpose and receipt of u tilisation Certificates are not maintained 
centrally in the Ministry of Finance. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Sir, it appears either this question should not 
have been accepted, or, the Finance Ministry should have decided not to reply to 
this question, because the reply says  that we know nothing about the 
autonomous bodies, we know nothing, we have to go to different Ministries. Then, 
it is just a waste of time to reply to this particular question. Sir, through you, I 
would like to inform the hon. Finance Minister, that at least 82 autonomous 
bodies have given the accounts in time, 144 autonomous bodies have not 
given the accounts in time, and 13 autonomous bodies are such which have not 
given even six months after, 11 autonomous bodies are such which have not given 
years after. Only 43 have done within one month, 45 within three months, and 
32 within 6 months. How will the hon.'Finance Minister like to improve the 
situation, so that these autonomous bodies give the accounts in time to the 
Ministries? 
9 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
SHRI P. CHIDAMBARAM: Sir, it is true that many autonomous bodies do not furnish 
the Utilisation Certificates within time. Therefore, from time to time, instructions have 
been issued to all the Ministries to insist upon Utilisation Certificates before fresh grants 
are released. In fact, there is a judgement of the Delhi High Court, in writ petition No. 6413 
of 2000 where by an order dated 18th March, 2003, the court directed that no further 
grants to any organisation are to be released, unless Utilisation Certificates in respect of 
previous grants were obtained. Following this judgement, the Ministry of Finance has issued 
an Office Memorandum to all the Ministries on the 5th May, 2003, bringing to their notice 
that this is the judgement of the High Court which is binding. You cannot release the 
grants unless the Utilisation Certificate to the previous grants are received in time. 
Nevertheless, we have noticed some violations in the case of half-a-dozen Ministries. Each 
one of those Ministries was told that you have violated the instructions, you have violated 
the order of the High Court; now, please rectify it. It is for each Ministry to ensure that the 
law is obeyed. We have repeatedly impressed upon the Ministries that they cannot release 
grants unless Utilisation Certificates are received. We will continue to impress upon 
them. 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA: Sir, my second supplementary is this. The Minister 
himself is saying that there are a number of autonomous bodies which are not giving

tax. There should be a mechanism. After a certain extent, you have to stop 
collection of taxes. So, some such mechanism should be introduced and to give 
some help to the poor man, come with a transparent proposal and the present 
mechanism has totally failed. What is the viewpoint of the Minister?

from the worst effects of the spiralling international prices, and the consequence of 
this is that our oil marketing companies have taken a hit of nearly 20,000 crores

THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR 
AIYAR): (a) The Central Finance Commission is required to make 
recommendations on the measures needed to augment the Consolidated Fund of the 
States to supplement the resources of the Panchayats on the basis of the 
recommendations of the State Finan ce Commissions. The Eleventh Finance 
Commission (EFC) had recommended grants of Rs. 8,000 crore for 
Panchayati Raj Institutions for the period 2000-2005. A Statement showing State-
wise release of grants as per EFC recommendations and their utilization by 
Panchayati Raj Institutions is enclosed as Statement-I (See below). The Twelfth 
Finance Commission has recommended Rs. 20,000 crores as grants for 
Panchayati Raj Institutions for the period 2005-2010. The State-wise allocation 
is enclosed as Statement-ll (See below). 
During the first Round Table of Ministers-in-charge of Panchayati Raj at 
Kolkata on 24-25 July, 2004, the subject of Effective Devolution of Finances was 
discussed. It was recommended that the "sound finances" of the Panchayats is 
a Constitutional obligation enjoined on the State by Article 243-I. In pursuance 
of the Constitutional obligation, the States and the Centre, in a true spirit of 
fiscal federalism should work together to strengthen the finances of the 
elected local bodies. To this  end, the devolution of finances to the three tiers 
of the Panchayati Raj System should be patterned on activity mapping for the 
devolution of functions and functionaries, thus securing effective devolution of 
powers to the PRIs through the linking of devolution of finances to the 
devolution of functions and functionaries. On the basis of the principles 
adumbrated above, the State Governments in the 7th Round Table held at Jaipur 
on 19 December 2004, agreed by consensus to prepare a road map to be made 
effective as soon as possible, and, in any case, by the end of the next fiscal 
year 2005-06 which will include the following components: 
1. Devolution, tier-wise and based on activity mapping, of: 
(a) Planning; 
(b) Budgeting; 
(c) Provisioning of finances. 
 
2. Inclusion of a PRI component in the budget of each State/Central 
Government Department based on activity mapping. 
3. Provision of progressively larger untied funds, tier-wise, to the 
Panchayats by State/Central Governments; 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
4.      Provision of untied grants from the Planning Commission to the PRIs, 
tier-wise, based on activity mapping. 
With respect to Centrally Sponsored Schemes (CSS), under the Sampoorna 
Grameen Rozgar Yojana (SGRY) allocation to the Panchayats is mandatory. In the 
case of other CSSs, the States are given an option to implement them through 
Panchayats. The SGRY is being implemented by the Ministry of Rural 
Development through Panchayats at the District Block and Village levels and 
resources are allocated in the ratio of 20:30:50 between these levels respectively. 
An amount of Rs. 4495.25 crores was allocated during 2004-05 under the SGRY. 
This was atso matched by the States' shares under this programme, which totalled 
to Rs. 1496.92 crore during that year. 
With respect to State Government a llocations to Panchayats, the direct 
financing of Panchayats varies from State to State and information thereof is 
available in the State Budget documents. 
(b) and (c) Grants under the Central Finance Commission are released to States 
keeping in view, the pace of utilization and fulfilment Of other conditionalities 
prescribed in the guidelines. 
As regards grants under the SGRY, the Ministry of Rural Development had 
introduced an Area Officer scheme which aims, at monitoring through field visits 
by its own officers of the major programmes of the Ministry, including 
SGRY, with special reference to quality, adherence to implementation of funds 
schedule, flow of funds, proper utilization of funds and achievement of physical 
and financial targets etc. Under this scheme, officers are assigned specific States 
for field visits and reporting. With a view to ensuring transparency and efficacy 
in the implementation of Rural Development Programmes, including SGRY, 
the Ministry of Rural Development has prepared a panel of National Level 
Monitors involving Senior Level Ex-Servicemen and Retired Civil Servants to 
monitor the policy and implementation environments of the programmes at the 
grass root level. National level Monitors  shall also be required to look into 
various specific complaints regarding implementation of programmes, as and when 
required by this Ministry.

(d) As per Article 243 J of the Constitution 'The Legislature of a State may, by Law, 
make provisions with respect to the maintenance of accounts by the Panchayats and the 
auditing of such accounts". Therefore, it is for the State Governments to introduce a system 
of internal audit and further to identify the agency to get the budget/funds of Panchayats 
audited. 
The Guidelines issued by the Ministry of Finance for the utilization of local bodies 
grants recommended by the Eleventh Finance Commission (2000-01 to 2004-05) provide 
that the C&AG shall be responsible for exercising control and supervision over the proper 
maintenance of accounts and their audit for all the three tiers/levels of PRIs and ULBs. 
State Governments should send a request under section 20(1) of the CAG(DPC) Act, for this 
purpose. As per the Guidelines, the format for the preparation of budgets and for keeping 
accounts for local bodies shall be prescribed by the C&AG This subject has been discussed 
further in the sixth Round Table of Ministers in charge of Panchayati Raj at Guwahati 
on 27-28 November 2004. A copy of the conclusions is enclosed as Statement-Ill (See 
below). 
The Sixth Round Table recommended that there is need to establish an internal audit 
system at every tier of the Panchayati Raj System and to regard C&AG-audit (or audit 
by bodies certified or technically guided by C&AG) as complementary external audit. 
Social audit has also been recognized as an important symbiotic complement to formal audit, 
essential for the sound and healthy development of Panchayati Raj. 
As regards SGRY, Ministry of Rural Development has informed that according to 
SGRY Guidelines, for every work sanctioned by District Panchayat/lntermediate 
Panchayat/Viliage Panchayat, there will be a Monitoring Committee of the Villagers of 
the areas belonging to the locality where the work is undertaken to ensure social audit and 
transparency at grass root level. The final report of such Committee would be attached 
along with completion certificate of the work and should also be placed in the next meeting 
of the Gram Sabha of the Panchayat where work has been executed  and also before the 
general assembly of the Intermediate/ District Panchayat if the work has been sanctioned 
by it.

Ministers in-charge of Panchayati Raj, and their representatives, bearing in mind 
the spirit of cooperative federalism which must inform the effective 
implementation of Panchayati Raj as set out in Part IX of the Constitution of 
India and related provisions, agreed to recommend to their respective 
Governments, for joint acceptance by the Centre and the States, the following 
points of action: 
Elections 
(i) The Indian voter is one and indivisible. The principle of parity between 
parliamentary and assembly elections, on the one hand and panchayat 
elections, on the other, must therefor e be maintained, especially as it is 
noticed that people's participation in panchayat elections is substantial 
and generally equal to or higher than in parliamentary/assembly elections. 
Thus, for example, even in States with difficult geographical terrain, 88% 
of the electorate has. participated in Panchayat elections in Himachal 
Pradesh and 83.5% has participated in Sikkim. 
(ii) While all matters relating to panchayat elections have been vested by the 
Constitution in State legislatures/Governments, there is a need to work 
towards commonality, if not uniformity, in election procedures and 
provisions. To this end, it would desirable to vest all responsibilities for the 
election process in State Election Commissions rather than splitting these 
up, including: 
(a) preparation of electoral rolls; 
(b) delimitation of constituencies;       
(c) reservations and rotations; 
(d) qualifications of candidates; 
(e) conduct of elections; and 
(f) functioning as the first stage of adjudication in election 
disputes. 
37 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
(iii) The Union Government might consider the preparation of a model code 
relating to the supervision, direct ion and conduct of elections to the 
Panchayati Raj institutions (PRIs). 
(iv) With a view to evolving a common electoral roll for all levels of 
elections, consolations between the Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) 
and the State Election Commissioners (SECs) might be encouraged 
with a view to resolving practical problems that might arise in the 
preparation, maintenance and updating of such electoral rolls for elections 
to be held at different times for different levels of Governments. The 
panchayat and nagarpalika wards should be regarded as the building 
blocks for electoral rolls for all levels of election. 
(v) Consideration may be given to incorporating in the laws pertaining to PR 
elections the same provisions of disclosure as apply to Parliament and State 
Assembly Elections. 
(vi) The Elections Commission of India (ECl) might be approached for 
establishing a forum for institutional interaction between SECs and ECl on 
issues such as directives being issued by the State Election Commission; 
the use of radio broadcasting for disseminating elections-related 
information; anomalies arising out of migration; linking delimitation 
with census operation; uniformity in service condition of SECs; and 
proposals like sealing the electronic chip in the Electronic Voting Machine 
( EVM), and not the machine itself, for evidentiary purposes, thus leaving 
the machine free for use in panchayat elections. 
(vii) States may consider according the same salary and emoluments to State 
Election Commissioners as High Court Judges are entitled to. 
(viii) It is recommended that the Delimitation Commission be regularly in 
contact with the SECs, who are members of the commission, to sort out 
practical difficulties arising out of delimitation process. 
(ix) To facilitate the use of Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) in panchayat 
elections, the Union Government in consultation with Election 
Commission of India and the SECs, might consider issues relating to the 
funding of the purchase of EVMs for the use of State Election 
Commissions. 
38 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(x) Elections to District Planning Committees provided for in Article 243ZD 
of the Constitution might also be brought within the purview of State 
Election Commissions to ensure full conformity with Constitutional 
provisions, which has not always been the case. 
Audit 
(i) Since local bodies are now institutions of local self-government, it is 
necessary to upgrade the work of the Director of Local Fund Audit 
(DLFA) and other similar bodies to the level required by Constitutional 
imperatives and, to this end, for DLFA and other similar bodies to work 
in concert with the Comptroller and Auditor General of India (C&AG). 
(ii) In recognition of PRIs being ins titutions of local self-government, PRIs 
themselves should be associated with the preparation of standards and 
norms and the emphasis should be on fund management and fund 
tracking, rather than simply on fund flow, to ensure greater 
accountability. 
(iii) In order to ensure that such audit contributes effectively to capping, 
reducing and eventually eliminating the scope for corruption in 
Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs) . it is necessary that audit & 
accounting standards appropriate to the work of the Panchayats be 
established and observed. These standards should be elementary, simple 
and easily comprehensible to the elected representatives, and should 
focus on; 
- when transactions should be looked into; 
- what should be monitored; 
- how the transactions should be documented; and 
- how they should be disclosed. 
(iv) There is need to establish an inte rnal audit system at every tier of the 
Panchayati Raj system and to regard C&AG audit (or audit by bodies 
certified or technically guided by C&AG) as complementary external 
audit. 
(v) Audit, to be effective, might include the establishment of a National 
Accounting Standards Board (NASB) for local government accounts and 
be complemented by the establishment of audit commissions 
39 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
or similar such regulatory bodies at the State level. 
(vi) Besides, arrangements may be made in State Legislatures for the establishment of 
Public Accounts Committees (PACs) specifically for PRIs or for the accounts of 
PRIs to be submitted to PR Committees of the State Legislatures. States level 
committees, as in Andhra Pradesh, for the settlement of audit paras may also be 
considered. 
(vii) It may be useful to complement such institutional arrangements by legislating an 
appropriate Fiscal Responsibility Act for elected local authorities. 
(viii) Outsourcing of accounting by such measures as village panchayats being authorized 
to employ certified Chartered Accountants against standard contracts might be 
considered. 
(ix) The training of both officials and elected representatives in sound accounting and 
audit practices is a high priority. To this end, State Governments are invited to 
make full use of the Regional Training Institutes (RTIs) functioning under the aegis of 
the C&AG, in particular the RTI at Kolkata which has been declared a centre of 
excellence; as also of the Institute of Public Auditors of India (IPAI). Substantial 
additional funding from the Union Government to facilitate training is high a 
priority. 
(x) Those State Governments which have not as yet availed of the arrangements for 
bringing the C&AG into the exercise of accounting and audit, including the C&AG's 
Technical Guidance and Supervision (TGS) Scheme for the PRIs, are invited to do so 
and the attention of all concerned is drawn to the publications of the Indian and 
Audit Accounts Department, in particular 
(a) Auditing Standards for PRIs and Urban Local Bodies 
(b) Guidelines for Certification of Audit of Accounts of PRIs 
(c) Training module of Audit of Gram Panchayats 
(xi) Given the shortage of staff for undertaking formal accounts and audit work in the lakhs 
of Village Panchayats, thousands of Intermediate Panchayats and hundreds of Zilla 
Parishads around the country, it is essential that automation and computerization 
of accounts be 
40 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
undertaken with all deliberate speed and to this end software like the one 
being prepared by the Xavier Institute of Management, B hubaneshwar 
for the Orissa State Government, for maintaining day-to-day accounts 
which is expected to be ready by early 2004, be deployed as widely as 
possible everywhere. 
(xii) Social audit is an important complement to formal audit and for the sound 
and healthy development of Panchayati Raj, it is essential to establish a 
symbiotic relationship between social and formal audit. 
(xiii) Social audit must necessarily be undertaken at the level of the Gram Sabha 
but might also be undertaken at higher levels of the Panchayat Raj system, as 
in West Bengal. 
(xiv) For social audit to be effective and based on the best practices available 
in different States, consideration might be given to the preparation of 
Social Audit Policies for adoption by State Legislatures/ Governments so as 
to provide a framework within which social audit is undertaken. Such 
Social Audit Policies may be targeted at facilitating popular participation 
in fighting corruption in Panchayats, as also complementing formal audit 
process by quality assessment, ascertainment of preferences and the 
provision of choices. At the same time, Social Audit Policies may 
provide for institutional measures to prevent needless harassment. 
(xv) To ensure appropriate follow-up to issues raised through social audit, 
legislative bodies and regulatory authorities might treat social audit 
resolutions on par with formal audit paras to ensure consideration and 
disposal within a time-bound framework. 
(xvi) Given the critical importance of total disclosure of information for 
effective social audit, States might consider passing Right to 
Information legislation, taking into account the legislation already on the 
books in such states as Rajasthan.

impact of new air service agreements on traffic at airports 
*651. SHRI R.P. GOEN KA: Will the Minister of CIVIL AVIATION be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently  India has signed two separate 
agreements with the UK and the USA to provide for unlimited number of air 
services in each other's territory; 
(b) if so, the details thereor, including restrictions, if any, on the points of call 
and/or destinations, in each of these agreements; and 
(c) the results of fresn review undertaken, if any, and the plans drawn up for 
upgrading/creating additional infrastructural facilities at the Indian airports to handle 
the increased numoer of flights? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF CIVIL AVIATION 
(SHRI PRAFUL PATEL): (a) and (b) Ye s, Sir. A revised Air Services 
Agreement between India and USA has been signed on 14th April, 2005 
replacing the earlier Agreement, wnich was signed in 1956. The earlier 
Agreement between india and USA already permitted either side to designate 
any number of airlines to operate air services between the two countries. While 
retaining this provision in the new Agreement, the revised Agreement also grants 
unlimited access to the designated airlines to any points of call in the territory ot 
the other country as against four airports under the earlier Agreement. Besides the 
revised Agreement also removes all restrictions on exercise of 5th freedom traffic 
rights, code snare rights and provides for greater operational flexibility. Removal 
of restrictions on points of call, code share rignts and 5th freedom rights 
would provide greater commercial opportunities to Indian carriers and would 
enable them to wean away traffic on India-USA route from third country carriers. 
As part of the on-going process to review traffic rights, bilateral talks with 
UK were held oo 12-13 April, 2005. As per the revised undertaking, 
entitlements on India-UK sector will go up to 56 services/week on Delhi/ 
Mumbai-London Heathrow route by winter season 2006. The increase in 
entitlements on these routes will be as follows:— 
(i) Winter, 2005 42 weekly services (ii) 
Summer, 2006 49 weekly services (iii)   
Winter, 2006     56 weekly services

of India may operate without any cap acity limit between India and UK. The 
designated airlines of UK may also operate on all other routes to India except 
Heathrow/Delhi and Heathrow/Mumbai subject to a total capacity limit of 7-
services/weeK to/from each airport in India, except that in the cases of 
Bangalore and Chennai, the total capacity limit will be increased to 14 
services/week each from the beginning of Summer, 2006. 
(c) Upgradation/expansion/deveiopment of airports is a continuous process 
and is undertaken depending upon traffic potential ana requirements from airline 
operators. Several measures are pres ently at hand to provide additional 
capacity/reduce congestion at various in ternational airports These include 
construction of taxi tracks, parking bays/stands on airside. Similarly domestic 
terminal capacity at Delhi and Mumbai airports are being expanded. 
International terminals at Delhi and Mumbai are being renovated. Steps are 
also being undertaken to introduce Common User Terminal Equipment, in-line 
baggage screening etc. at several airpots for quick facilitation of passengers. Air 
traffic management systems are also being reviewed to increase aircraft 
movement. 
Closure of Oil Industries Training Cell 
*652. DR. ALLADI P. RAJ KUMAR: Will the Minister of PETROLEUM 
AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the Oil Industries Training Cell which imparted training for 
checking adulteration in motor fuel has been closed; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; and 
(c) in the absence of the training cell, who is looKing after this work? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) and (b) The Government have neither created nor 
wound up any cell by the name of "Oil industries Training Cell" to impart 
training for checking adulteration in motor fuel. However, M/s Bharat 
Petroleum Corporation Limited (BPCL) have reported that one of the retired staff of 
the Oil Coordination Committee (OCC) had approached them during 1996-97, 
offering to conduct training sessions on anti adulteration and using the term 
"Oil Industries Training Cell" for such training. On this request, M/s. BPCL 
provided him office space in their Chennai office and 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
as and when required, he was invited to conduct training sessions. He vacated 
this office space on 31.12.2003. 
(c) The training of oil industry officials on product knowledge, quality 
assurance and anti-adulteration issues is an ongoing activity. Such training is 
imported by the public sector Oil Ma rketing Companies (OMCs) to their 
officials in their training institutes. OMCs also discuss these issues at various 
forums/meetings. 
The steps taken by the Government/OMCs in containing the adulteration in 
motor fuels include the following: 
(i) Under the Control Orders issued by the Government to prevent fuel 
adulteration, under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, State 
Governments are empowered to take action against those indulging in 
adulteration. Government have taken up this matter with all the State 
Governments/Union Territory Ad ministrations to step up 
inspections/surprise checks to ensure that adulteration related activities 
are minimized and to exercise vigil/conduct inspections at various private 
firms, factories, processing units, etc., under their jurisdictions so as to 
indentify the perpetrators of adulteration and take stringent action against 
them within the available legal framework. 
(ii) OMCs undertake regular and surprise inspections of Retail Outlets and 
also take action under Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) and 
Dealership Agreements against those indulging in adulteration and 
malpractices. MDG provide for penalty of termination of dealership in cases 
of adulteration being established. 
(iii) As advised by the Government, Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have 
created a separate wing to report to a Director other than Director (Marketing), 
which will oversee and monitor all activities and operations to curb adulteration 
and specify norms and guidelines in this regard. 
(iv) Keeping in view the misuse/diversion of SKO for adulteration, the import 
of SKO by private parties has been canalized through OMCs. 
(v) OMCs have introduced new tamper proof tank-truck locking systems to 
prevent en-route adulteration by transporters. 
(vi) IT solutions like monitoring movement of  tank trucks through Global 
Positioning System (GPS) and monitoring level of fuel tanks in Retail 
Outlets through retail automation are being introduced. 
48 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(vii) Branding of Retail Outlets and third party certification of Retail Outlets have been 
initiated by the OMCs. 
(viii) A pilot project has been approved for strengthening the distribution network of PDS 
kerosene with a view to working towards ensuring that this product is made 
available to the targeted consumers and is not diverted for adulteration. 
Measures to check adulteration are kept under continuous review of the 
Government.

†4994. SHRI RAVI SHANKAR PRASAD: 
              DR. MURLI MANOHAR JOSHI:

†Original notice of the question was received in Hindi. 
92 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) when was such decision taken by Government; and 
(d) the reasons for taking such decision? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM): (a) to (d) The Management of operational risk is a 
real and live issue for modern-day banks, particularly in view of the decision by the 
Basel Committee on Banking Supervision ( BCBS) to introduce a capital charge for 
this risk as part of the new capital adequacy framework (                Basel-ll). The 
BCBS has also issued a Paper on Sound Practices for the Management and 
Supervision of Operational Risk in February 2003. This paper has highlighted the 
importance of the role of the banks' Board as under: 
(i) The board of directors should be aware of the major aspects of the bank's 
operational risks as a distinct risk category that should be managed, and it should 
approve and periodically review the bank's operational risk management 
framework. The framework should provide a firm-wide definition of 
operational risk and lay down the principles of how operational risk is to be 
identified, assessed, monitored, and controlled/mitigated. 
(ii) The board of directors should ensure that the bank's operational risk management 
framework is subject to effective and comprehensive internal audit by operationally 
independent, appropriately trained and competent staff. The internal audit function 
should not be directly responsible for operational risk management. 
Since the New Capital Adequacy Framework requires banks to hold capital 
explicitly towards operational risk as also the felt need for banks to manage operational 
risk, RBI has issued a 'draft' Guidance Note on the management of operational risk 
and placed it on the website for wider dissemination in March 2005.

India's growth potential 
5010. SHRI VIJAY J. DARDA: Will the Minister of FINANCE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the ADB India Economic Bulletin 
108 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
published articles wherein it has been predicted that India is slated to become 
the third largest economy with a share of 14.3 per cent of global economy by 
2015 and that it would graduate to become the third pole and growth driver by 
2035; 
(b) if so, whether our economic planning strategies being oriented towards 
achieving that goal; and 
(c) if not, what are his views to this economic growth anticipated in the ADB 
India Economic Bulletin? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (SHRI 
S.S. PALANIMANICKAM) (a) Yes, Sir The ADB India Economic Bulletin 
(January, 2005) of the Asian Development Bank, India Resident Mission, in its 
Special Feature article "The World Economy: From Unipolar to Tri-polar" has 
indicated that India's share in worl d Gross Domestic Product (GDP) at 
purchasing power parity (PPP) would increase from 8.2 percent in 2015 to 11.2 
percent in 2025 and to 14.3 percent by 2035. The feature indicates that by 2015, 
it would be a bipolar economy with China becoming the largest economy, ahead 
of USA. By 2025, the Indian economy is projected to be 60 per cent the size of 
the US economy. As the share of USA in world GDP falls and that of India 
rises, India will emerge as the third pole in the global economy. According to this 
Bulletin, the transformation into a tri-polar world will be completed by 2035 with 
the share of GDP at purchasing power parity for China, USA and India at 
30.0 per cent, 16.0 per cent and 14.3 per cent respectively. 
(b) and (c) Economic growth in term s of PPP, which is used in this 
Bulletin as an indicator of growth is not generally used to measure growth. 
However, achieving high and sustained growth has been our objective and our 
policies and strategies reflect this objective India has been taking measures to 
accelerate growth through enhanced investment, infrastructure facilities, accelerating 
growth of industries and human resource development to achieve sustained long 
term growth.

Closure of Anti-Adulteration Cell 
5055.    SHRI AMAR SINGH: 
              SHRI ABUASIM AZMI:  
             SHRI R.K. ANAND: 
           SHRIMATI PREMA CARIAPPA: 
Will the Minister of PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that adulteration of petrol and diesel is a big-ticket scam that 
involves as annual recurring loss of at least Rs. 10,000 crore to the Exchequer; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that public sector oil companies are also involved in 
that scam; 
(c) if so, the details thereof and what is Government's reaction in regard thereto; and 
(d) whether it is a fact that anti-adulteration cell in the Ministry had been disbanded 
and if so, what are the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF PETROLEUM AND NATURAL GAS (SHRI MANI 
SHANKAR AIYAR) (a) While Government is aware of attempts by unscrupulous 
elements to adulterate petroleum products, no definitive estimate of the annual loss to the 
exchequer on this account is available. 
(b) and (c) To the best of Government's knowledge and information, Public Sector Oil 
companies are not involved as Corporate entities in any such scam. Any individual/official 
caught in any such act of malfeasance is proceeded against. 
Action taken by the Government/Public Sector Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) 
towards containing the menace of adulteration include the following:— 
(i) Under the Control Orders issued by the Government to prevent fuel adulteration, 
under the Essential Commodities Act, 1955, State Governments are empowered 
to take action against those indulging in adulteration. Government have taken up 
this matter with all the State Governments/Union Territory Administrations to 
step up inspections/surprise checks to ensure that adulteration related 
146 

{10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
activities are minimized and to exercise vigil/conduct inspections at various 
private firms, factories, processing units, etc., under their jurisdictions so as to 
identify the perpetrators of adulteration and take stringent action against them within 
the available legal framework. 
(ii) OMCs undertake regular and surprise inspections of Retail Outlets and also take 
action under Marketing Discipline Guidelines (MDG) and Dealership 
Agreements against those indulging in adulteration and malpractices. MDG provide 
for penalty of termination of dealership in cases of adulteration being 
established. 
(iii) As advised by the Government Oil Marketing Companies (OMCs) have created 
a separate wing to report to a Director other than Director (Marketing), which will 
oversee and monitor all activities and operations to curb adulteration and specify norms 
and guidelines in this regard. 
(iv) Keeping in view the misuse/diversion of SKO for adulteration, the import of 
SKO by private parties has been canalized through OMCs. 
(v) OMCs have introduced new tamper proof tank-truck locking systems to prevent en 
route adulteration by transporters. 
(vi) IT solutions like monitoring movement of tank trucks through Global Positioning 
System (GPS) and monitoring level of fuel tanks in Retail Outlets through retail 
automation are being introduced. 
(vi) Bonding of Retail Outlets and third party certification of Retail Outlets have been 
initiated by the OMCs. 
(viii) A pilot project has been approved for strengthening the distribution network of 
PDS kerosene with a view to working towards ensuring that this product is made 
available to the targeted consumers and is not diverted for adulteration. 
Measures to check adulteration are kept under continuous review of the 
Government. 
(d) The Anti-Adulteration Cell (AAC), was created in March 2001 under the aegis of 
the Ministry of Petroleum & Natural Gas (MOP&NG). It was found to be ineffective 
and its officers possibly involved in undesirable activities. Therefore, a one-man 
committee under the chairmanship of Additional Secretary, Ministry of Petroleum & 
Natural Gas was set up in 
147 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
April, 2004 to conduct an extensive review of the working of AAC. The 
report showed that the AAC with its existing structure & functions could not 
play a meaningful role in the effort s to curb the menace of adulteration. 
Accordingly, the cell was wound up in July 2004.

   Policy on proper utilisation of water 
5103. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA : Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are considering the formation of a policy for 
proper utilization of water in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have any proposal to store the water which flows 
into the sea through rivers in times of flood and excess rains; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRI JAI PRAKASH NARAYAN YADAV) (a) to (d) National 
Water Policy-2002 provides for proper utilisation of water in the country. 
Relevant para of the National Water Policy, 2002 are as under: 
3.1 Water resources available to the country should be brought within the 
category of utilizable resources to the maximum possible extent." 
192 
• 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
3.2 Non-conventional methods for utilization of water such as through inter-
basin transfers, artificial recharge of ground water and desalination of 
brackish or sea water as well as traditional water conservation practices 
like rainwater harvesting, including roof-top rainwater harvesting, need 
to be practiced to further increase the utilizable water resources. 
Promotion of frontier research and development, in a focused manner, 
for these techniques is necessary. 
3.4 Watershed management through extensive soil conservation, 
catchment-area treatment, preservation of forests and increasing the 
forest cover and the construction of check-dams should be promoted. 
Efforts shall be to conserve the water in the catchment. 
3.5 Water should be made available to water short areas by transfer from 
other areas including transfers from one river basin to another, based on a 
national perspective, after taking into  account the requ irements of the 
areas/basins. 
To achieve the above objectives appropriate schemes are formulated by the 
State Governments as per their priorities. The Ministry of Water Resources has 
also recently taken up a pilot scheme on "National Project for Repair, Renovation 
and Restoration of Water Bodies directly linked to Agriculture" and as scheme 
on "Artificial Recharge to Groundwater and Rainwater Harvesting" is also 
under active consideration.

Need to fill up vacancies and increase strength of Judicial 
Officers in Subordinate Courts and Judges of High Court in 
Andhra Pradesh 
DR. ALLADAP. RAJKUMAR (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, an independent and 
impartial judiciary in a democratic polity like ours secures its citizens 
justice in an impartial manner. We have subordinate courts, High Courts 
and the Supreme Court for this purpose. It is true that justice delayed is 
justice denied. But, if justice is delayed due to shortage of Judicial Officers 
and Judges, the matter becomes serious. That is exactly what is happening 
in our country. In support of it, I wish to highlight the case of my home 
State Andhra Pradesh. In the subordinate courts, the number of sanctioned 
posts of Judicial Officers is 797, but only 724 Judicial Officers are working, 
which means, 73 posts are vacant, and nearly one million cases are pending 
in these courts. 
[MR. DEPUTY CHAIRMAN in the Chair] 
Similarly, there are 12 vacancies of Judges in the High Court of Andhra 
Pradesh. Out of 39 sanctioned posts, only 27 judges are there. Nearly two 
lakh cases are pending in the High Court. This is also the case in the 
entire country. I, therefore, demand that— 
a. fill up all the vacant posts of Judicial Officers in the subordinate 
courts and those of judges in the High Court of Andhra Pradesh 
immediately; 
b. increase in the sanctioned strength of Judicial Officers and 
Judges so that pending cases are substantially reduced within a 
definite timeframe; 
c. and, lastly, release Central grants to Andhra Pradesh, if financial 
constraints are hampering appointment of Judicial Officers and Judge, 
or, increase their sanctioned strength so as to ensure that justice is not 
delayed to millions of people, at least, in Andhra Pradesh. Thank you, Sir.

Concern over depletion of ground water level and shortage of drinking 
water in the country 
SHRI GIREESH KUMAR SANGHI (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, our planet consists 
of 70 per cent water. Out of which 97 per cent is available in the form of seas 
and, the rest, in the form of glaciers, river basins and other sources. In India, 
annual water availability is 1869 billion cubic metres (BCM), out of which only 
432 BCM is ground water. With the ever increasing requirement of growing 
population, the per capita availability has fallen from 5177 cubic metres in 1951 
to 1820 cubic metres in 2001. This is a dangerous sign. 
To improve the ground water level, the Government should make efforts to 
improve infiltration of ground water from the rainfall by adopting modern technology 
practices which have been proved successful in other countries. 
215 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
The other fact is that 80 per cent of water available is used for agriculture 
and, the 20 per cent, for industrial and domestic requirements. 
We face failure of rains almost every year, as a result we come across 
power cuts, shortage of drinking water, etc., in most parts of the country. 
The Government should make serious and sincere efforts to find out a 
lasting formula to the vexed problem of non-availability of drinking water, 
depletion of ground water, power cuts and such other problems related to 
water. 
Linking of rivers would be a lasting solution for resolving the water problem. 
A formula should be framed for sharing of water between the States in a 
proportionate manner. An expert committee should be set up to go into 
the depleting ground water and submit ways and means to improve the 
ground water level. 
Demand for establishment of a Super-speciality Post-graduate 
Medical Institute in Chhattisgarh 
SHRI MOTILAL VORA (Chhattisgar h): Sir, Chhattisgarh having a 
population of more than two crores needs super-speciality medical institute. 
Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru Hospital, Bhilai, which has thousands of crores 
of immovable property, about 400 acres of land and all functioning super-
specialities recognised for post-graduation by D.N.B. can cater to the 
requirements of super-speciality institute. 
This will also help in offering the be st medical care to the whole of 
Central India including Chhattisgarh. Research for diseases and 
opportunities for training in super-specialities to medical graduates and 
post-graduates could also be taken care of. 
The proposed institute will have several new features like the holistic 
system and international collaborat ion and paramedical training. The 
Ministry of Health should consider the demand. 
Demand for substitution of the Word 'DAFLA' by 'NYISHI' in the 
constitution (Scheduled Tribes) order 1950 
SHRI NABAM REBIA (Arunachal Pradesh): Sir, the Arunachal Pradesh 
Legislative Assembly in its session held on 19th August, 2003, has passed 
a resolution that the name of DAFLA tribe be substituted by NYISHI 
216 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
including PUROIK and BANGRU as Sub-tribes in the Constitution 
(Scheduled Tribes) Order 1950. In my maiden speech on 18.12.1996 on 
the topic—the Constitution (55th Am endment) Act, 1986, (the State of 
Arunachal Pradesh Act, 1986) on the floor of this House, the Government 
was urged upon to remove this lacuna from the Statehood Act. A number 
of correspondences have been made by the State Government in this 
regard but without any positive outcome. 
The Nyishis are the largest single tribe spread over East Kameng to 
Upper Subansiri districts of Arunachal Pradesh. A sizeable number of Nyishi 
population reside in North Lakhimpur and Darrang districts of Assam. 
Word "DAFLA" has acquired pejorative overtones, is not an Arunachal 
word, and hence considered derogatory. Their forefathers "ABOTANI" did 
not come across such a word. A necessary amendment to the Constitution 
in the Monsoon Session of Parliament for substitution of this derogatory 
word is demanded. 
Concern over fall in the prices of tea 
leaves in the country 
SHRI A. VIJAYARAGHAVAN (Kerala): There are thousands of small 
sized tea growers and also lakhs of labourers dependent on this sector. 
The tea farmers particularly the small and medium size farmers in the 
country are confronted with a very serious situation due to the continuous 
fall in the prices of fresh tea leaves. The farmers are getting the lowest 
prices for many years. About 90 per cent of the small-scale farmers belong 
to Nilgiri. In Nilgiri it is just Rs. 4 per kg against a production cost of 
approximately Rs. 10 per kg. The situation is very precarious, as many 
farmers have been forced to commit suicide, because they were unable to 
withstand the financial crunch. Therefore, the Government has to intervene 
immediately. The authorities concerned had assured positive measures to 
the agitating farmers and people but failed to implement the assurance 
given. 
The free trade agreement with other tea producing countries like Sri 
Lanka has led to large-scale import of tea even while sufficient quantity of 
tea leaves are produced in the country. The situation has dealt a severe 
blow to the small-scale farmers. Although the prices of the finished tea 
217 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
products could improve marginally in the recent months, it did not reflect on the 
prices of the fresh tea leaves. In fact, the prices continue to keep a downward 
trend. 
I urge upon the Government to intervene in this matter to protect the 
interests of the thousands of small-scale farmers and lakhs of labourers, make 
arrangement for procurement of green tea leaves by the Government agencies, 
declare a Minimum Support Price at least Rs. 15 per kg and also review the 
free trade agreement with countries like Sri Lanka. 
Concern over environmental degradation caused due to illegal mining in 
Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY (Pondicherry): Sir, Mathura suffers as illegal mining 
ravages natural bounty. Thousands of people inhabited in the hilly northern belt 
home to the folklore of Hindu God Krishna are waging a grim campaign to save that 
land from illegal mining and stone quarrying. 
The Braj region, encompassing Mathura town in Uttar Pradesh, the densely 
forested Bharatpur in Rajasthan and Faridabad in Haryana, are rapidly losing 
their natural identity due to indiscriminate and illegal mining for sandstone. The hills 
are being blasted down with dynamite and pulverised to dust, allegedly without 
official sanctions, and residents are getting desperate. Hunger strikes and 
protest rallies by villagers taking on not only the miners but also U.P. and 
Rajasthan Governments. Much of the mining is affecting not only the Shrine but it 
will have its impact on the Taj Mahal in Agra also. In the process forest species 
are also being killed or driven out. It is a grave irony that the 5000-year-old 
heritage hills of Braj, far older than the Taj, are being completely neglected. 
A villager of the affected area near Bharatpur featuring five historic Jain temples 
stated that these mines are not giving jobs and most the work is done by 
machines. 
Therefore, the people of the villages in Mathura region and Bharatpur region 
have said in one voice that if we do not act now, we will repent for centuries. 
Therefore, it is high time that the Central Government and the Ministry of 
Environment and Forests acted immediately in collaboration with the State 
Governments of Uttar Pradesh and Rajasthan for curbing illegal mining 
activities in those areas.

Concern over custodial deaths in the country 
SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA(Rajasthan): Sir, I rise to draw the attention 
of this House to the growing trend of custodial deaths in the country. It is 
extremely disturbing that such incidents are increasingly taking place 
even in relatively peaceful areas with generally stable law and order situation. 
The victims were not exactly the history-sheeter criminals. Custodial deaths 
of under-trials have trivialized the Rule of Law by the law-enforcing agencies 
themselves as they showed utter disregard for the human life. The two 
incidents of 15th and 16th March, 2005 in Delhi and more recently another 
custodial death in the Tihar Jail indicate the callous impunity with which 
human rights were violated without taking any cognisance of the pleas of 
victim's relatives. As reported elaborately in the media, in one case the 
deceased was himself earlier rescued from kidnappers but died in the 
police custody. While in the second case the victim was arrested and 
beaten up fatally for an offence that actually never occurred. In both the 
cases the reported course of events made the close complicity of local 
police rather evident. Trust of local ci tizenry is the cardinal principle of 
civil policing. The police is the repository of public's trust in fair law and 
order. Its presence should be reassuring for common man. Instead citizens 
are now considering the presence of police as a hostile intrusion. There is 
an urgent need for police to redeem the public trust. I call upon the 
Government to take affirmative and preventive steps to contain recurrent 
violations of citizen's rights.

SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I wish to bring to 
the notice of the House a matter of urgent public importance. As everybody 
is. aware, the State of Andhra Pradesh has been severely affected by a 
series of droughts during the last few years. This has led to a situation 
where farmers have to borrow money from village money-lenders, at 
exorbitantly high rate of interest, eventually falling into a debt trap. 
It is absolutely necessary to bring about a major shift in the policy of 
granting loans to farmers. Presently, the poor and honest farmers, who 
are already debt-ridden, have to go through a complex procedure for securing 
loans from banks by keeping their land as collateral. 
This is a very peculiar situation, because in urban areas, housing and 
225 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
car loans are sanctioned very easily. Cars loans are approved in less than 24 
hours, but that is not the case with loans given to farmers, who have to walk long 
distances on foot to the nearest bank several times, before a loan is granted. 
Moreover, rates of interest on urban housing loans are much less than the 
agricultural loans. Housing loans come at an average of 7.5 per cent, while 
farmers are presently paying an average of 9.5 per cent interest. 
It is, therefore, necessary that whenever an area is declared as drought-affected, 
as is the case in many districts of Andhra Pradesh, interest on outstanding 
loans has to be waived. Thank you.

The Private Security Agencies (Regulation) Bill, 2005 
THE MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL): Sir, I beg to 
move: 
"That the Bill to provide for the regulation of private Security agencies and for 
matters connected therewith or incidental thereto, be taken into 
consideration." 
As the Members are aware, in recent years, there has been a proliferation of 
private security agencies in India. This is due to the expansion in the number 
of business establishments, growing incidents of crime and increasing 
demands for security. The resources of the Police are limited 
226 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
and they cannot meet the demand for security services on the scale 
required. While private security agencies have helped meet the need of 
business establishments for security of their personnel and property, yet, 
there has been growing concern about t heir functioning; many of these 
agencies conduct their operations without consideration of proper standards, 
and if left unchecked, can have adverse security implications. There is 
also the danger of private security firm employees encroaching upon the 
duties of the Police by way of wearing uniforms, which resemble those of 
the Police and using weapons in an illegal manner. The Government 
proposes to introduce a legislation for regulating functioning of the private 
security agencies. As would be noticed, the main objectives of the Bill are 
to set proper norms for functioning of the Private Security Agencies in the 
country and also to bring uniformity, as far as possible, in regulations of 
Private Security Agencies. The salient features of the proposed legislation 
include inter alia: (a) Licence mandatory: No person shall engage in the 
business of Private Security Agency supply Security Guards unless he is 
a holder of a Private Security Agenc y licence issued by the Controlling 
Authority in accordance with the provisions of the Bill and the rules made 
thereunder. The licence will be valid for five years and is renewable. Any 
existing private security agency, wh ich has been operating before the 
commencement of this Act, shall also obtain a licence and also ensure 
the required training to its security guards and supervisors within a period 
of one year from the date of such commencement, (b) Services by the 
private security agencies: The private security guards may be with or without 
arms and "armoured car service" can also be provided by the private security 
agencies for security of movement of Bank's cash and other valuables. As 
for the licensing authority, the State Governments shall designate an officer 
not below the rank of Joint Secretary in the Home Department of the State 
• or an equivalent officer to be the controlling authority for the purpose of the 
Bill. 
As regards the provision about persons not eligible for licence, a person 
shall not be considered for issue of licence under this Act if he has been 
convicted of an offence in connecti on with promotion, formation or 
management of a company, any fraud or misfeasance committed by him 
in relation to the company, including an undischarged insolvent; or, convicted 
by a competent court for an offence, the prescribed punishment for which 
is imprisonment for not less than two years; or, keeping links with any 
organisation or association, which is banned under any law on account of 
227 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
1.00 P.M. 
their activities, which pose threat to the national security, or, public order; 
or, there is uniform information about such person indulging in activities, 
which are prejudicial to national security, or public order; or, dismissed, or, 
removed from Government service on grounds of misconduct or moral 
turpitude. 
A company, firm, or an association of persons shall not be considered 
for issue of company license under this Act if it is not registered in India; 
or, having a proprietor or a majority shareholder, a partner or an Director, 
who is not a citizen of India. 
Coming to training, imparting of prescribed training to the security guards/ 
supervisor has been stipulated in the Bill. As for cancellation or suspension 
of licence, the licence can be cancelled/suspended by the controlling 
authority on the violation of the provisions of the Bill. However, opportunity 
will be given to the licence holder to present his case before the licence is 
cancelled. 
As regards the appellate authority, the Bill provides for preferring appeal 
against refusal to grant licence and cancellation of licences. The Home 
Secretary of the State shall be the appellate authority. As for offences and 
penalties, penalty of fine/imprisonment have been provided in the event of 
the security agencies violating the provisions of this Bill. 
Sir, I hope that the Private Security Agencies (Regulation) Bill, 2005, 
will be approved by all sections of the House. I commend this Bill for 
consideration and passing in this House.
