because they are not trained. They really do not know what is actually the 
requirement of the job. People from rural areas come to towns in search of 
employment, and these private security agencies deploy them on very 
meagre salaries. They do not provide un iformity in training to all these 
security guards. The security guards deployed by these private agencies 
lack awareness of the security arrangements. At times, Sir, they adopt 
lackadaisical approach, and some of them seem to be functioning in a 
state of lassitude. Sir, another worriso me dimension is the intrusion of 
anti-social elements in these organisations. Of course, we all know that 
such agencies are set up by retired defence or police officers, or certain 
officers, who had the privilege of dealing with the subject while being in 
service. Retired defence personnel find it an apt retirement profession to 
dabble in. Sir, I am sorry to say that in some cases we find that even 
dismissed employees, dismissed Governments servants, have barged into 
this sector. Because no licence is required and there is no check on 
them. Sir, there are instances of guards, deployed by these private security 
agencies, abetting crime. There were reports when security guards of a 
very prominent company were involved in the burglary, in the embezzlement 
of cash from the Reserve Bank of India. There were also instances, when 
it was found that armed guards, deployed by these agencies, had fake 
gun licences. Recently, there was a news-item that one of the very important 
agency, I would not like to name it, was involved in the fabrication of records 
of the guards deployed in a public sector undertaking. And they defrauded 
worth crores of rupees from where they were charging. So, these are the 
reasons. That is why an enactment of a codified law is absolutely essential 
232 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
to control this issue because these associations have a nexus with the 
maintenance of law and order in this as well as detection of crime. Sir, 
compliment the Home Minister. He has explained in detail the manner in which a 
licence will be given, the conditions for granting a licence, the conditions for 
cancellation of licence and so many other things. I would not like to go into all 
these things in detail. Even, the condition of employment of security guard, 
especially mentioned in sub-clause 2 of Section 10 will have salutary effect. He 
has also mentioned the eligibility, ineligibility cancellation of licence, etc. Sir, the 
Bill spells out the eligibility of a licence, ineligibility of a licence, modalities for 
processing the application, etc. Sir, the Bill also provides strong statutory 
framework to the functioning of such private agencies and making them 
accountable to a suitable mandatory mechanism. Sir, the Bill empowers the 
State Government through a medium of controlling authority, to be appointed by 
the State Government. Sir, these are very laudable provision, but I have some 
suggestions to make. 
Sir, I will first touch upon clause 4. It is a very good clause. Then comes, clause 
5, which says, "an application for issue of a licence under this Act shall only be 
considered from a person after due verification of his antecedents." It is a very 
good clause. This will overcome the undersirable people jumping into the business, 
cheating the people and making money under the garb of private agencies. But, 
Sir, because the licence will be given after the verification of the antecedents, in 
the case of a company, there will be two, three or four directors and if one or two 
directors retires or leaves, there is no provision whether they will be forced to 
have the antecedents of that company also verified or not. It only provide that 
the licence will be issued after verification, but there is no provision as such that 
in case, there is a change in the directorhsip or proprietorship of that company, 
the antecedents will be reverified or not. What will be the status of that company? 
What will be the position of that company during that interim period? Sir, that is 
not there. Then, Sir, sub-clause (d) of section 6 says, "Dismissed or removed 
from Government service on grounds of misconduct or moral turpitude." Sir, 
does this include local bodies and PSUs? It only says, 'dismissed employees 
from Government'; local bodies and PSUs do not come under the purview of the 
Government as such, because in the Acts that have been mentioned, It's not 
mentioned whether the Local Bodies Act will also apply here. Then, Sir, in clause 
7(2), there 
233 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
is, "ensure the availability of the training for its private security guards." Of 
course, there is no mention here, but, I am sure, while framing the rules, 
care will be taken to fix the period of training. Training can be for one 
month, two months, three months or six months. There should be uniformity 
of training incumbent upon all the agencies to go through that. Sir, then, 
there is sub-clause (2) of clause 10, which say, "No person who has been 
convicted by a competent court or who has been dismissed or removed on 
grounds of misconduct or moral turpitude while serving in any of the armed 
forces of the Union, State Police Organisation, Central or State Governments 
or in any private security agency shall be employed or engaged as a 
private security guard or a supervisor . Sir, there is a catch here-while 
serving in any of the Armed Forces of the Union, State Police Organisation, 
Central or State Government or in any private security agency. Why the 
words 'security agency' have been mentioned? Why not 'any private firm'? 
What is the provision for that? If a person is dismissed for misconduct, 
embezzlement or anything from a private company, he will be entitled for a 
job. But if he is dismissed from a private agency, what would be his lot? 
that aspect also needs to be looked into. Then, a question which arises 
is, whether the PSUs are covered under this clause or not. The hon. Member, 
Shri Penumalli Madhu, was referring to sub-clause 3 of clause 10, that is, 
whether preference should be given to the unemployed you or not. Sir, all 
unemployed youth seek jobs. So, th ere cannot be a reservation or 
preference for unemployed youth. In the matter of providing employment, 
every youth is equal. What I want to suggest here is this. It should have 
been like this. Preference will be given to the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled 
Tribes and OBCs. That sub-clause should be inserted here. 
Then, I come to a very important clause, that is, clause 13. It says: The 
Controlling Authority may cancel any licence...Sub-clause (h) of clause 
13(1) says, 'that the licence holder is or has wilfully failed or refused to 
render the services agreed to anyperson.' I am sure, when the rules are 
framed, there should be a mention or there should be a rule that whenever 
a private agency offers services and all that, there should be a proper 
agreement. Otherwise, how will one de cide that the person refused to 
provide the services? What will be the criteria of judging whether it has 
been done or not? 
Now, I come to sub-clause (k) (iii) of clause 13(1). It says that when the 
private security guard or guards provided by the private security agency 
234 

[10 May, 2005] RAJYA SABHA 
were found habitually drunk or indisciplined, the licence will be cancelled. If 
a guard wants to sort out the enmity with the employer, then certainly, he 
will come drunk and he will indulge in indiscipline. So, on the basis of this, 
how can the misbehaviour of a guard or guards to sort out their enmity, to 
sort out their differences with the employer, their licence be cancelled? This 
needs to be looked into or elaborated. The same is the case with clause 
13(1), sub-clause(k) (v) which says: Had connived or abetted a crime against 
the person or property placed under their charge. Here also, if a guard 
commits the mistake, if the guard commits this offence, how can the licence 
be cancelled? This sub-clause also needs to be looked into very carefully. 
Now, I come to clause 16 It says: The Controlling Authority or any 
other officer authorised by it in this behalf may at any reasonable time, 
enter the premises of the private security agency and inspect and examine 
the place of business, the record s, accounts and other documents 
connected with the licence and may take copy of any document. It is a 
very good clause, Check on the agencies is very essential. But, Sir, there 
are two catches. One is, we are empowering one nominated officer of the 
level of Joint Secretary to enter the premises of any agency. But there is 
another thing also because, this will also lead to repercussions if only one 
officer is authorised to decide, and there is no appeal against that, there is 
no appellate authority against that. He is not to take permission of any 
higher authority. There should be some provision that he is to take the 
permission from some higher authority. The controlling authority will be 
the Joint Secretary. If he decides, there can be conflict of business rivalry. 
If a particular firm approaches the Joint Secretary-I am not casting any 
aspersion-this does happen in life that such and such agency should be 
barred or should be defamed. They will raid their office and find out 101 
things. But there is another things. In case the agency refuses to 
cooperate, what will the Joint Secretary, while sitting in his office, do? 
There should be a provision that in case the agency refuses to cooperate, 
then warrant for entering the premises should be obtained from the court. 
That is what is required. 
SHRI V. NARAYANASAMY (Pondicher ry): The office r should be 
above the rank of Joint Secretary. He should be either a Secretary or an 
Additional Secretary. 
SHRI R.K. DHAWAN: The Contro lling Authority should have the 
permission of an officer higher than him in rank to enter the premises. 
235 
■ 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
Then there will be checks and counterchecks. Sir, sub-clause (3) of clause 
18 is very disturbing: 
"If violation of any law is noticed by any private security guard during 
the course of discharge of his duties, he shall bring it to the notice of his 
superior, who in turn shall inform the police either through his employer or 
agency or on his own." 
Sir, I fail to understand what is the meaning of this. If a guard is employed 
there, how can he decide whether any law of the country is being violated 
or not? If he is unhappy with the employer, does it mean that he will go 
straightway to the police saying that such and such person, say, R.K. 
Dhawan, is violating the law? Because he is being employed by me, what 
authority has he got to decide that? He may be educated or uneducated. 
How an a guard deployed by me sit in judgement that I am violating such 
and such law? And that too, such a wide thing If he notices any law being 
violated, and if he reports it to the superior officer or if he goes straightway 
to the police, it will have a very bad effect, Sir, in the long run. 
There are some other suggestions also. I have already mentioned about 
the promoter. About the period of training also, I have spoken. About the 
preference also, I have made a suggestion. 
There is another clause. The provision in clause 10(2) should be amended 
by stating that a person who is fa cing criminal charges would not be 
eligible. Here again, we are introducing the concept that a person who is 
not found guilty earlier can be found guilty. If a person is involved in a 
criminal offence and if he is facing criminal charges, he will be going to the 
court. At times, he will not report fo r duty because he has to go to the 
court. What credence will I put on him? How can I understand that he is a 
good man, who himself is facing criminal charges? Sir a provision should 
be made in this Bill that any person who is facing a criminal case—I am 
not saying an ordinary case—will not be deployed. How can I employ that 
person? How can I know anything about the guard sent by the agency? I 
do not know whether that person is facing a criminal case or not. He might 
have a criminal mind; he may indulge in a criminal offence. So, all these 
things are there. 
Then, Sir, this Bill punishes the licence holders for a variety of offences. 
Mr Madhu has also spoken about it. But hardly any punishment is 
236 

[10 May, 2005]                       RAJYA SABHA 
prescribed for violations made by the individual security guard. An individual security 
guard commits a mistake and gets away. He is simply dismissed by the employers. 
There should a provisions in the rules that if an individual security guard is found 
guilty, he will be covered under such and such criminal laws. About this also, 
Sir, Mr. Madhu said, "What will happen if the Central agency decides to close 
its office?" Its licence may not be cancelled. If some defaulter decides to close 
the agency, Sir, such an agency should give information, in advance, in that 
regard, They should not be allowed to close the agency unless and until they pay 
all the dues to their employees. That is very essential. 
Sir, there is a provision that a guard will become ineligible if he is punished for less 
than such and such period. Why can't a person become ineligible to be a 
appointed a guard irrespective of the period of sentence? If a person is 
convicted, he is convicted. How can I deploy a person who has been convicted of 
an offence, the sentence for that, probably, is less than six months? But the fact 
remains that he is a convicted person. I won't have trust in him.Cover all those 
things, Sir. There should be a provision in the rules that persons who are convicted of 
any offence will not be deployed. 
Sir, last but not the least, for the employees working at the lowest rung of 
security guards, their guarding hours and pathetic salaries, of course, they have 
mentioned that they will be covered under the various Acts. Sir, those who are 
exploited are well educated, well built youths, in desperate search of jobs. I know 
there are many persons in my own locality, who are graduates, postgraduates. 
They are doing duties, but, Sir, they are paid very meagre salaries. And; day-in-
day-out, they are in search of their jobs; they are not serious about their duties. 
They always tell me, "Sir, I am an M.A.. Why can't you get me some job 
somewhere? So, I think their salaries should be fixed according to their 
qualification. Something must be done for them. The last point is that a new section 
should be incorporated to establish a suitable mechanism for rating the services 
provided by these agencies. How can we create an agency which is not 
conforming at all to the standards? He has got a licence because he is eligible. 
Then also their should be some mechanism to arrive at the rating. This kind of 
rating is done in every system, in every field, here also it should be done. With 
these suggestions, I support the Bill moved by the hon. Home Minister, Thank 
you.

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Nadu): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, in 
the recent past, the Gorkhas, who migrated from Nepal, were employed 
for safeguarding our houses and work places, But, now, there are a 
number of business establishments and private institutions. Increasing 
threat to life and property, and escalating public violence and domestic 
violence have heightened the need for seeking the service of private security 
agencies, which are specialised in offering security services. These private 
security agencies are meeting the security needs of the business 
houses, since the Police Force is already burdened with the law and 
order duties other obligations. Since there is a mushroom growth of the 
private security agencies, they have to be regulated; otherwise, they may 
pose a serious security threat becasue the private security personnel may 
involve in criminal activities. So, this Bill has been brought forward to 
regulate the functioning of these private security agencies which are now 
accountable to a regulating mechanism. 
[THE VICE-CHAIRMAN, SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA, in the Chair.] 
The State Government authority has to issue the licence to these agencies, 
after observing certain legal norms, as per this Bill, Under the provisions of 
this Bill, preference can be given to a person who has served in the Army, 
Navy, Air Force, Police Force and Home Guards in the hope that they 
have the required training, experience and vigilant nature to meet the 
challenges. This is an agreeable provision. At the same time, unemployed 
youths from the SCs, STs and OBCs should also be given a chance by 
these service, agencies. According to the provisions of this Bill, the private 
security guards are prevented from using uniforms of the Navy, Army, Air 
Force and the Police Force. This is also acceptable. Since the private 
security guards are issued photo identity cards, they should also be provided 
with some kind of a uniform other than the one used by the Army, Navy, Air 
Force and the Police Force so that they can be identified as private security 
guards. This is missing in this Bill. Therefore, I submit that this lacuna has 
to be rectified. With these words, I conclude. Thank You.

SHRI RAMAMUNI REDDYSIRIGIREDDY(Andhra Pradesh): Sir, I rise to 
support the Bill brought before the House by the hon. Home Minister. This Bill 
should have been brought much earlier looking at the increasing activities of the 
private security agencies in the country. Anyway, better late than never. The 
objectives of the Bill are laudable as the private security industry now encompasses 
an extensive range of occupations and activities that includes door supervisors, 
suppliers or installers of security equipment, private investigators, security 
consultants, security guarding services, provider of protected forms of 
transport and suppliers and installers of safes, amongst others. It is also 
important because there have been instances where some persons working 
with private security agencies were found to be conducting not only 
espionage for Pakistan-based agencies, but are also involved in various heinous 
crimes. This law is very necessary in the absence of any uniform policy for private 
security agencies in the country. For example, in a city like Delhi, the agencies 
have to register themselves with the Delhi Police Licensing Branch. But, when it 
comes to other States, the guidelines vary. So, there is a need to have a uniform 
law to control, monitor and look at the activities of the private security 
agencies in the country. 
Now, I wish to offer some comments on some of the clauses of the Bill. Sir, 
clause 4 of the Bill deals with regularisation of private security agencies and issue of 
licences to private security agencies. Clause 6 deals with rejection of issue of 
licence to persons who are convicted or having links with banned organisations 
or dismissed from the Government service, etc. Okay. If you are not giving licence 
to above persons what the ineligible person will do is, he will apply for licence in 
the name of his spouse, son or relative and they will get licence and will remain 
dormant and the person who has been barred will run the affairs of the agency 
from behind the scene. How are you going to control such persons? You have 
also not given any qualification for a person to start a private security agency. You 
are only verifying his antecedents under clause 5. Nothing else. So, I request 
that some professionalism has to be injected into the Bill at appropriate place 
which should say that only such and such person, having such and such 
qualification or experience or professionalism is eligible for 
247 

RAJYA SABHA [10 May, 2005] 
starting a private security agency. Otherwise, this Bill is not going to control the 
mushrooming of private security agencies which lack professionalism. 
The Bill prescribes Rs. 5,000 as licence fee if the security agency is 
operating in one district; Rs. 10,000 if it is operating upto 5 districts; and Rs. 
25,000 if it is operating in the entire State. I would like to know the basis of 
fixing this amount. On what basis are you fixing this licence fee? Is it fixed one 
time licence fee or are you going to do for a particular period of time? Is this fee to 
be paid again when the renewal is done? It has to be made clear. 
Sir, clause 8 deals with renewal of licence and you are saying that the 
Controlling Authority shall pass an order for renewal of licence within a period of 
30 days. But, if the Controlling Authority fails to renew the licence within the 
prescribed period of 30 days, what will happen to the agency which is providing 
private security service? Should it stop its operations? So, I would request the 
hon. Minister to make this provision clear. You say that the Controlling Authority will 
pass an order for renewal within 30 days. If he fails to pass, you make it clear that 
licence deemed to have been renewed. 
The most important thing about private security services is 
professionalism and training. The more professional and trained you are, the best 
the results would be. Under Clause 9(2) you are asking them to impart training 
and skill to its guards. I do not know what kind of training these private security 
agencies will provide to their guards since they do not have the necessary 
paraphernalia, professionalism, infrastructure, etc. So, I submit for consideration of 
the hon. Minister that why not think of imparting professional and other 
necessary training to private security guards in our police training institutes since 
we have the professionalism, infrastructure and expertise by charging some 
amount. This can also be made mandatory by inserting a clause in the Bill itself. 
It is good that have made in the Bill itself that preference should be given to 
armed force personnel, paramilitary forces or armed constabularies. But if you look at 
the eligibility criteria to becomea private security guard, it seems to be amusing. 
Clause 10 (b)says that one has to be in the age groups of between 18 and 65 
years. And, sub-clause (e) of the same clause says that he has to fulfil such 
physical standards as may be prescribed. My point is,on the one hand you are 
allowing a person, say, of

man of 60 years to fulfil the physical standards and complete security

clause and restructure sub-clause (b) of clause 10 by prescribing the age

If one reads the Bill, it is clear that  Controlling Authority is the sole

not included this in the present Bill. So, Sir, these are some of the views,

over them and make the necessary changes in the Bill to make it more 
effective and implementable. Thank You. 
SHRI R. P. GOENKA(Rajasthan): Mr. Deputy Chairman, Sir, I rise to 
support this Bill. Before lunch-break, the Minister had given very good 
explanations and took out many of the doubts which we had. However, I 
would like to make a few suggestions. 
The first suggestion is that the Bill should indicate the conditions in 
which the security guards will be permitted to use arms and the regulations

while on duty. Otherwise, in today's world, we see many mafia kings moving 
about and they will have a security guard and they will shoot bang, bang, 
bang. That will go on. One thing which the Bill has missed is, if a security guards 
gets injured or killed during duty, what precaution or what compensation he is 
entitled to? About the training of the security guard, few of the previous 
speakers have already mentioned to employ the unemployed youth in the 
security guard forces. It is not the answer. They must have training and when 
they wish to join the security guard forces, they should be most welcome. Sir, the 
last point that was elaborated by Mr. Dhawan in Section 18, Clause 5, Sub-Clause 3 
was that a security guard can go and complain to his superior and that superior can 
come and enter the premises of the office or his residence. It is very dangerous. 
I would like to recollect and I will tell you, Sir that many years ago in income Tax 
Act such a clause was there. Anyone can enter. After a lot of debate, persuasions, 
that clause was taken out. Here, we are reintroducing it. And who is that man? He 
is a security guard who is supposed to protect me. Instead of protecting me he 
goes and makes a report and a Joint Secretary of a State says, 'okay' and that is it 
Where is my privacy? Sir, this clause was elaborated by Mr. Dhawan. I don't want 
to repeat it. But I am sure the Minister would keep it in mind while framing the 
final Bill. With these words, I support the Bill and endorse it and compliment 
the Minister for bringing out such a Bill.

SHRI SHIVRAJ V. PATIL: Sir, I would like to thank the hon. Members for the 
support they have given to this Bill. This Bill was also introduced in the House in 
1994 for the first time. Then, it was withdrawn. It was referred to the Standing 
Committee. Again, it was introduced; then again, it was withdrawn. And 
ultimately, now Sir, this is before us. 
      [MR. CHAIRMAN in the Chair]  
I am very happy that we are likely to pass this Bill in this House and may be 
in Lok Sabha also, in this session. Many good points have been made. We will 
consider these good points while using this Bill, while implementing or 
enforcing this Bill. Under this law, we have to make rules also. While making rules, 
many points which have been made by the hon. Members will also be borne in 
mind so that what they have expressed

here, are reflected in the laws that will be used in this respect. Sir, the first point, 
which was made by the first speaker, was about the job security of the security 
guards. It is exactly for this purpose we have mentioned in the Schedule some of 
the laws which are useful in this respect. The laws which are mentioned in the 
Schedule give the protection to the security guards who would be employed by 
these agencies. The Payment of Wages Act, 1936, the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947, The Minimum Wages Act, 1948, the Employees' Provident Funds and 
Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952, the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965, the Contract

The Equal Remuneration Act, 1976 and the Inter-State Migrant Workmen 
(Regulation of Employment and Conditions of Service) Act, 1979. All these laws 
are going to provide security to the security guards. So, there should be no 
apprehension on this point. However, the first speaker mentioned that why should 
we not have the Workmen's Compensation Act in this Schedule. It seems that this 
suggestion is a very valid suggestion, and I am inclined to say that it should be 
mentioned in the Schedule. The law provides that this Schedule can be changed 
by the Government, and it is not necessary to introduce one or two laws in this 
Schedule to come to the Legislature for that purpose. So, the Government is 
given that authority, and under that authority, we will examine it, and I think, it 
should be there. I would like to get It examined and introduce it so that the 
compensation is available to the security guards. 
Sir, the second point which was made was about the compensation and all 
those things. This point was made by many Members. If the Workmen's 
Compensation Act is there, under that Act, the compensation can be given to the 
security guards who may suffer while discharging their difficult duties. 
The third point related to clause No. 13, and it was said: why do you

because, if you have to cancel the licence which is given to the agency, it 
should not be lightly done, and I think, this clause gives the grounds on which 
the licence can be cancelled. I do think that this clause

point of time, I would like to say that let this amount of money be there, and if it 
is found that this is too small an amount, we can take a decision about it later

One of the Members wanted to know whether this law will be 
applicable to the agencies or to the individuals also. This law is going to be 
applicable to the agencies and not to the individuals. If any individual is wanting to 
provide security to anybody, and the person to whom the security is to be provided, is 
willing to take him as his guard, there is going to be no difficulty. There is no law 
which says that one person should not protect the life or the limb or the property 
of any other person. But if there is going to be an agency, consisting of many 
persons having weapons and things like that, and providing the security to the 
other individuals, that agency should be guided by certain rules and certain 
principles. And if that agency is not fulfilling those conditions, that agency will not be 
allowed to carry on that kind of duty. So, there is no difficulty is allowing any 
individual to provide security to anyone else. 
One question was raised, and it was a right question, that there can come 
up proxy agencies. One individual can take a licence and another individual can 
run that agency. The individual who can be given the licence will make the 
application, will get the licence, but the individual who cannot make the 
application and cannot get the licence may run that agency. What happes if 
this kind of eventuality arises? This is exactly why we have provided that if any 
agency is working not according to this law, and other laws but contary to the 
laws, the licence given to the agency can be cancelled. It it is found out that the 
person who has received the licence is not running the agency, that licence can be 
cancelled. That person should not have been given the licence for running the 
agency, Once this fact comes to the notice of the Controlling Authority, the 
Controlling Authority can take action against him. 
About the cancellation of licences, well, there are grounds given here and the 
licences can be given in certain circumstances. The kind of provision

SHRI SANTOSH BAGRODIA(Rajasthan): Sir, I would just go through two-
three points quickly. One is regarding Recommendation No. 28. Some of the

cannot afford good legal aid, while in the custody. 
The second point is about Recommendation No. 13. The lowering down of the 
standard of proof as recommended in the Malimath Committee will also make 
the investigating agency slack and lazy and they will not do their investigation

guilt without any reasonable doubt and the poor person who is accused will be

prohibitive fees.
